summary: RTP allows header extensions, but it was hard to use many of them. This document provides a general mechanism for using a small number of small extensions in each RTP packet, where many extensions are possible and registration is decentralized. Which ones are in use is negotiated per session.

eli5.summary: It gives each audio or video packet a few tiny optional sticky notes, and the two sides agree beforehand which notes they will use.

questions: how do rtp header extensions work
one byte vs two byte rtp header extension
subtitle: A way to carry several small, named extensions in each RTP packet header, agreed on through SDP.

tldr.problem: The original RTP header extension allowed only one extension per packet and gave no guidance on how its 16-bit identifiers should be allocated without collisions.
tldr.mechanism: Packets carry a sequence of small extension elements, each with a local ID and a length, in a one-byte or two-byte form. SDP extmap attributes map each local ID to a URI that names the extension.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 5285 and now allows one-byte and two-byte forms in the same RTP stream, negotiated with extmap-allow-mixed.

today: RFC 8285 is a Proposed Standard from October 2017 and obsoletes RFC 5285. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a General Mechanism
sections.content:
RTP lets a packet header carry an extension, but the original format permits at most one extension per packet, identified by a 16-bit identifier and a 16-bit length in 32-bit words. It also gives no help in allocating the identifiers so they do not collide.

RFC 8285 allows multiple extension elements in one packet, named by URIs. It defines an IANA registry for extensions defined in IETF specifications, and an SDP method for mapping between the URIs and the identifiers carried in packets. It applies to RTP/AVP, the Audio/Visual Profile, and its extensions.

The goal is a simple mechanism where extensions can be used without formal registration yet without collisions. It offers an alternative to burying metadata in the media bitstream, and the RFC says that where a higher-level mechanism exists it can be used instead, but otherwise an RTP-level one is better than tying metadata to one media format.
sections.eli5: An RTP packet used to have room for only one sticky note and no rules for numbering them. Now it can hold several, each with an agreed number.

sections.title: Rules for Header Extensions
sections.content:
Whether a header extension is present, and what it means, is negotiated or defined out of band, for example in SDP. The 16-bit identifier values used here are only an architectural constant for tools like network analyzers; the negotiation is the definitive indication.

The extensions must not break non-extended receivers. A header extension MUST NOT change the meaning of standard RTP header fields or RTCP. It MAY carry additional metadata, provided the RTP layer works if that metadata is missing. The RFC notes that data also sent in RTCP can be sent as a latency optimization, and that using the Media Identification (MID) extension with SDP BUNDLE may lose some application functionality if the MID is missing while the RTP layer is unaffected.

Each element has a local ID and a length. IDs MUST be negotiated or defined out of band, there are no static allocations, each distinct extension MUST have a unique ID, and ID 0 is reserved for padding. The header extension SHOULD only be present when a packet has elements, and an element SHOULD only be present when needed.

For delivery, the RFC suggests tailoring the number of repetitions to the loss probability. With N repetitions and packet loss probability P, the target delivery probability is 1-P^N. Feedback such as RTCP can show when to stop repeating.
sections.eli5: The sticky notes must be optional extras. If a receiver ignores them, the call should still work, just like ignoring a note on the side of a package.

sections.title: One-Byte and Two-Byte Forms
sections.content:
In the one-byte form, the RTP "defined by profile" field MUST be 0xBEDE. Each element starts with a byte holding a 4-bit ID (1 to 14) and a 4-bit length that is the number of data bytes minus one, so 0 means one byte of data and 15 means 16 bytes. ID 15 is reserved: if it is seen, the length is ignored and processing of the extension stops, considering only the elements before it.

In the two-byte form, the profile field is 0x100 followed by a 4-bit appbits field. Each element has an 8-bit ID (1 to 255) and an 8-bit length counting data bytes only, where 0 means no data. There is one ID space for both forms, so IDs 1 to 14 mean the same in either.

Padding bytes have the value 0 and MAY appear between elements or after the last one, since the total length is counted in 32-bit words. All receivers MUST support the one-byte form, which is preferred. Transmitters SHOULD NOT use the two-byte form when all elements fit the one-byte form. A stream MUST use only one form unless all recipients are known to support mixing, though one packet carries only one form.
sections.eli5: The small form is a tiny label with a short note, and the big form allows longer notes. Both use the same numbers, and zero bytes are just blank filler to keep things lined up.

sections.title: Naming and Mapping with SDP
sections.content:
Each extension is named by an absolute URI that precisely identifies its format and meaning. URIs that contain a domain name SHOULD also contain a month-date in the form mmyyyy. For extensions defined in RFCs, the URI SHOULD be a URN starting with urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:. The URIs do not have to be dereferencable, which allows confidential or experimental use.

An SDP attribute maps each local ID to a URI: a=extmap:<value>["/"<direction>] <URI> <extensionattributes>. The direction is sendonly, recvonly, sendrecv or inactive. Each ID may be used only once per media section, or once at session level, and mappings must be either all session level or all media level. When SDP is used, the presence of extmap is the sign that this style is in use, not the magic number in the packet.

To allow mixed forms, the attribute a=extmap-allow-mixed takes no value and can be used at session or media level. An offerer who wants both forms MUST include it, and an answerer who supports and wants it includes it too. Without both, mixed forms MUST NOT be used in the same stream.
sections.eli5: Each sticky note gets a long unique name, and a list sent before the call says "note number 1 means this, note number 2 means that." That list is what both sides use to read the notes.

sections.title: Offer/Answer Negotiation
sections.content:
In an SDP Offer/Answer exchange, the extmap can carry directions to allow one-way use, mutually exclusive alternatives, or more extensions than fit. If an extension is offered as sendonly and the answerer wants to receive it, it MUST mark it recvonly in the answer. An answerer that does not want or understand an extension SHOULD remove it, or may mark it inactive to show future interest. Local identifiers must not be remapped by a session update, which may change directions or add or remove extensions.

To offer mutually exclusive alternatives, or more extensions than the valid range allows, the offerer MAY use identifiers in the extended range 4096 to 4351. The answerer SHOULD choose, and remap the chosen ones to a free identifier in the valid range.

With SDP BUNDLE, all "m=" lines in a group share one ID space. The same extension URI and configuration offered in multiple lines MUST use the same ID, while a difference in extension attributes normally requires different IDs.
sections.eli5: When two people set up a call, one lists the notes it would like to use and the other says which ones it wants. Numbers over 4095 are spare slots for options that get renumbered during the chat.

sections.title: Security, Registry and Changes
sections.content:
The document defines only a place to carry information, so the security implications of each extension must be discussed with that extension. Because use is negotiated with RFC 3264, integrity protection and end-to-end authentication MUST be implemented. Header extensions have the same security coverage as the RTP header, which under SRTP is unprotected or integrity protected, so integrity protection SHOULD be used to prevent DoS attacks such as changing the extension. RFC 6904 provides a way to selectively encrypt header extensions in SRTP.

IANA keeps the "RTP Compact Header Extensions" registry under Expert Review, and the reviewer checks things like public availability, that the extension can be ignored without breaking RTP, and that it contains a security analysis. It also registers the extmap and extmap-allow-mixed SDP attributes.

Compared with RFC 5285, the main changes are mixed one-byte and two-byte support via the new attribute, the revised statement that an extension "may be ignored", more text on transmission, and an expanded Security Considerations section.
sections.eli5: The notes are not secret by default, so bad actors could mess with them. Locks and tamper seals should be used if the notes matter.

fields.name: ID
fields.desc: Local identifier, 1 to 14; 0 is padding and 15 is reserved.

fields.name: len
fields.desc: Data bytes that follow, minus one.

fields.name: length
fields.desc: Length of the extension data in bytes; 0 means no data.
